quarterly_data.quarter: PDF Solutions press release: Introducing Exensio Aurora: PDF Solutions Unveils (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: PDF Solutions unveiled Exensio Aurora, a new Exensio analytics architecture built to handle semiconductor manufacturing data at petabyte scale and to deploy agentic AI across manufacturing operations and the supply chain; the company says it began investing in it more than a year ago at the urging of several of its customers. Its distributed engine 'is designed to deliver approximately 25X faster performance at comparable hardware cost', with a Manufacturing Data House for 3D and higher-dimensional data, model lifecycle management built on Kubernetes (central training with deployment to OSATs, test floors and edge boxes) and LLM-enabled agents with on-premise options. CEO John Kibarian ties it to 3D architecture and hybrid packaging creating a larger and more complex global supply chain; PDF says that in most cases less than 5% of semiconductor manufacturing data is analyzed with conventional tools. Availability: first available in September 2026 as a beta release for a small number of early adopters; first public demonstrations at PDF Solutions CONNECT 2026 on October 15-16.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately 25X faster performance at comparable hardware cost; beta for early adopters in September 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Management is decidedly more optimistic on H2 than at the Q1 call: the wafer-allocation doubts voiced in Q1 have eased because of the deep TSMC relationship ('we have more chance to get upside capacity'), and by late Q1/early Q2 the company found TSMC support and customers' capacity commitments much firmer. Cloud-related shipments (cloud compute, cloud training, cloud connectivity) were close to 80% of Q2 shipments with the remaining ~20% consumer/crypto/memory-related; the H2 mix should be similar, with crypto fading toward nothing and automotive ramping in its place. Versus last year, China's share of revenue declines (absolute volume still up), while the US share and Taiwan share both increase. Full-year gross margin: still confident, but dependent on customers' production ramp success and whether NRE tape-outs land this year or slip to next year.

quarterly_data.signal: Pre-payments rose notably in Q2 because GUC pre-buys materials for large CSP turnkey programs - besides CoWoS it must secure HBM stacks and substrate ahead of the build so everything (substrate, HBM, the SoC from TSMC) arrives together for packaging. GUC sells the customer the finished CoWoS package with HBM inside; if HBM prices rise the chip price rises with it, so the cost risk sits with the customer, not GUC. Management cited HBM pricing going from about 240 at the start of the year to 700 and up to 900 (as spoken; unit not stated), fully passed through. Whether HBM procurement flows through GUC's own P&L or is booked as a service fee is still being worked out case by case at this early stage.

quarterly_data.signal: North America CPU customer: GUC has won the next-generation project; the next chip is expected to reach volume production around the end of this year / early next year, while the current project has been shipping for almost two years. Next year's wafer capacity allocation is being opened up by TSMC over the coming 1-2 months and management is 'very optimistic', though the outcome depends on TSMC capacity and the customer's own forecast. Management is confident the customer will keep outsourcing back-end physical design even as it builds in-house capability, because one product line spans too many SKUs to take fully in-house. Automotive: the China automotive customer (combined cockpit+ADAS single chip, taped out around October-November last year) should start contributing revenue next year; for the North America automotive customer GUC did the current-generation tape-out and is in talks for the next generation, with the volume timing dependent on that customer's robotics plans.

For HBM base die, memory makers currently keep the logic die to themselves (Samsung using its own logic process, SK Hynix working with TSMC); GUC sees its opening coming when a memory maker's main product splits into many SKUs, and notes its existing cooperation with SK Hynix on other product lines has been good.

quarterly_data.quarter: GUC (Global Unichip) press release: GUC Announces 2nm 16 Gbps HBM4E IP (09-22-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: GUC announced that its HBM4E PHY and Controller IP is design-ready and has been adopted in customer AI ASICs (customers not named). Implemented on TSMC's N2P process, the HBM4E PHY has taped out on TSMC CoWoS-L advanced packaging. Building on GUC's silicon-proven 12 Gbps HBM4 IP on TSMC N3P, the HBM4E IP pushes data transfer speeds up to 16 Gbps across all signed-off operating conditions (GUC claims industry-leading power efficiency and a compact area), with its proprietary interposer layout optimized for SI/PI across TSMC CoWoS packaging configurations. A face-up variant is engineered as a bottom die in TSMC SoIC-X, with dedicated TSVs for signal pull-out and feedthrough power delivery to top dies; the IP incorporates proteanTecs interconnect monitoring. CTO Igor Elkanovich said uniting face-up HBM, face-up UCIe and GLink-3D IPs gives GUC a complete interface IP portfolio for 3D SoIC architectures.
quarterly_data.figure: HBM4E up to 16 Gbps on TSMC N2P (from 12 Gbps HBM4 on N3P); PHY taped out on CoWoS-L; adopted in customer AI ASICs

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: mature-node supply has moved from cyclical swings to an irreversible structural tightening - 8-inch and 12-inch mature capacity has become a strategic resource, global capacity expansion lags demand, and shortages of labour, materials or capacity are the new normal, so foundry pricing has long-term support rather than being a short-lived phenomenon. Faraday's value is shifting from design technology (now only the entry ticket) to full value-chain management: capacity booking, wafer allocation, packaging and test capacity coordination and cost management. On 2027: mature-node capacity for Q4 2026 is already very full and will squeeze into Q1 2027 for both 8-inch and 12-inch; management expects next year to be as tight as this year and, given the UMC relationship, sees Faraday benefiting as it did during the pandemic, with a higher chance of securing capacity - calling it the best timing for Faraday.

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: most of the advanced-packaging mass production originally planned for H2 2026 has been deferred to next year. Reasons: customer-supplied SoC dies arrive too slowly (validation problems, some needing re-spins that take another three to six months); one customer's HBM procurement has slowed; and OSAT capacity, especially engineering resources, is tighter and supports Faraday less than expected. Customers understand and will not easily cancel the related orders, and the packaging capacity booked for them is kept. Advanced packaging will miss this year's plan, but MCU and mature-node ASIC MP make up for it, so the full-year revenue target can still be met; the CEO remains positive on next year. Timelines: when the customer supplies the SoC die, MP used to take about a year and now more than a year, even two; when Faraday designs the die, MP takes at least two years. Management expects 2 to 3 such projects in 2027 and most of the packaging projects to reach mass production next year. On OSAT capacity favouring large customers, the CEO said the projects will reach MP smoothly but with longer lead times, citing decades of cooperation with the OSATs and capacity booked as a package with customers.

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: advanced-node and advanced-packaging project intake is steady; complex NRE SoC designs have long lead times, so this does not yet show in NRE revenue, but the pipeline under negotiation is more positive. It is pursuing several cloud-related advanced-node projects; in communications it targets OCS switches among others, and in Q2 it won a project in an OCS switch, with other cases in progress. Revenue contribution is still small and many projects expected to enter MP may slip into next year. The customer base is shifting quickly toward US and European customers, which lifts margins. Under tight capacity, OSATs are less willing to support small-volume, engineering-heavy projects, so Faraday targets higher-quality projects to win OSAT support.

quarterly_data.signal: CEO on the nearly three-year Intel Foundry collaboration: phase one was 18A validation - Faraday taped out an 18A test chip last year, validating the process kit and building physical-design experience. Phase two: Intel now promotes 18A-P (an upgraded 18A) to outside customers; 18A is for Intel's internal use while 18A-P is open to external foundry partners. Faraday has downloaded the 18A-P PDK 1.1, completed the internal environment setup with the reference flow running, and is porting its ecosystem to 18A-P. Phase three is winning real design-service / turnkey projects: this month Faraday reached a milestone, providing design services to an Intel Foundry partner to implement 18A-P - the amount is not yet large, but it is a real implementation. Faraday holds regular meetings with Intel roughly every one to two weeks.

quarterly_data.signal: CEO on the UMC-Intel 12nm collaboration: the first revenue benefit for Faraday is 12nm IP development (IP licensing), followed by 12nm ASIC. Management describes the 12nm fab as US-based with scale and geographic advantages, making local production and the North American market easier to address. Faraday's IP is built almost entirely on UMC 14nm and will be replicated to the Intel 12nm node quickly; it expects to start engaging UMC 12nm customers in the second half of next year. The playbook mirrors 28nm, where Faraday has taken on 100+ chips: owning its IP makes its NRE quotes very competitive. On IP licensing, 12nm is the main driver (high unit price, and a new node needs a full build from foundation IP to function IP); with 18A-P and the UMC 12nm process, Faraday expects two strong new product lines from next year.

Operating expenses $18.4 billion, up 19% on increased R&D. Diluted EPS $2.84, up 19%; record operating cash flow $53.9 billion. Greater China up 38% year over year (best iPhone quarter in history there). Installed base more than 2.5 billion active devices. December tariff cost landed at roughly the $1.4 billion outlined. Cook: iPhone gained share in December, and Mac gained share for full calendar year 2025.
quarterly_data.figure: $143.8 billion revenue (up 16%); iPhone $85.3 billion (up 23%); gross margin 48.2%; EPS $2.84

quarterly_data.signal: Apple Silicon as the AI platform. Cook: Apple products are 'far and away the best platforms in the world for AI. That's in no small part because of the extraordinary power and performance of Apple Silicon.' The M5-powered 14-inch MacBook Pro 'takes a huge leap in AI performance thanks to the next-generation GPU architecture and a faster neural engine'; iPad growth was 'driven by the M5-powered iPad Pro and the A16-powered iPad'. Cook: 'the majority of users on enabled iPhones are actively leveraging the power of Apple Intelligence' (dozens of features, available in 15 languages). Enterprise pull: AstraZeneca 'is rolling out over 5,000 M5-powered iPad Pros to its pharmaceutical sales team to take advantage of AI capabilities, including Apple Intelligence'; Snowflake 'has deployed over 9,000 Mac devices company-wide'. The AI-capable share of the installed base is 'a growing number' (CFO declined to give a figure).
quarterly_data.figure: over 5,000 M5-powered iPad Pros (AstraZeneca); over 9,000 Mac devices (Snowflake)

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: A LEADING-EDGE NODE SHORTAGE GATES THE MARCH QUARTER. Cook: 'we exited December with very lean channel inventory due to that staggering level of demand. And based on that, we're in a supply chase mode to meet the very high levels of customer demand. We are currently constrained and at this point, it's difficult to predict when supply and demand will balance. The constraints that we have are driven by the availability of the advanced nodes that our SoCs are produced on. And at this time, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal.' Asked why Apple is constrained (the analyst framed it as advanced packaging), Cook named the node: 'it's the advanced nodes that we, like three nanometer to be specific, where our SOCs are the latest SOCs are produced on is what is gating the Q2 supply', 'a direct result of the 23% growth' far outstripping internal estimates, with 'more limited flexibility in the supply chain for some period of time'. The March-quarter revenue outlook of 13% to 16% 'comprehends our best estimates of constrained iPhone supply during the quarter'. Cook declined to comment on supply beyond Q2.
quarterly_data.figure: 'three nanometer' advanced nodes gating Q2 supply; March-quarter revenue outlook of 13% to 16% includes constrained iPhone supply

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: FIRST READ ON THE MEMORY COST CYCLE. Cook: 'memory had a minimal impact on Q1. So the December gross margin. We do expect it to be a bit more of an impact to the Q2 gross margin and that was comprehended in the outlook of 48 to 49%... we do continue to see market pricing for memory increasing significantly. As always, we'll look at a range of options to deal with that.' Asked whether long-term agreements or spot buying is the answer for memory: 'It's a range, and so I don't want to get more specific than that. I mean, there are different levers that we can push, and who knows how successful they'll be'. Asked whether raising prices is a lever: 'I wouldn't want to speculate on that one.' CFO: the March gross margin guide is similar to the December level, with favorable services mix partly offset by a seasonal loss of leverage.
quarterly_data.figure: memory impact minimal in Q1, 'a bit more' in Q2 within the 48 to 49% gross margin outlook

quarterly_data.signal: March-quarter (Q2 FY2026) outlook, assuming tariff rates and policies in effect as of the call: total company revenue to grow 13% to 16% year over year (including constrained iPhone supply); services revenue growth similar to the December-quarter rate; gross margin between 48-49%; operating expenses between $18.4 billion and $18.7 billion (higher R&D year over year); OI&E around $100 million; tax rate around 17.5%. quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: GOOGLE BECOMES THE FOUNDATION FOR APPLE'S MODELS. Cook: 'we are also collaborating with Google to develop the next generation of Apple foundation models. This will help power future Apple intelligence features, including a more personalized Siri coming this year.' 'We basically determined that Google's AI technology would provide the most capable foundation for Apple Foundation Models... We'll continue to run on the device and run-in private cloud compute.' Terms undisclosed ('we're not releasing the details of that'); 'you should think of what is going to power the personalized version of Siri as a collaboration with Google.' Compute: on-device and private cloud compute are both important ('we don't see it as an either-or'); on data center capacity for Siri, Cook: 'we've done the sort of the best job that we can do, and I've and either have or are putting capacity in for it.' Apple is 'shipping servers to power Apple Intelligence from our new manufacturing facility in Houston.' CFO: CapEx follows a hybrid model - on tooling and data centers Apple leverages 'a combination of first and third-party capacity'; CapEx 'can be volatile', and December-quarter results included CapEx for the private cloud compute environment built out last year.

quarterly_data.quarter: Apple press release: The new Mac mini and Mac Studio are available today (09-22-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Apple's new Mac mini and Mac Studio became available starting September 22, 2026, powered by new Apple silicon: Mac mini with the all-new M6 and with M5 Pro, and Mac Studio with M5 Max and the all-new M5 Ultra. M6: 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, the all-new Dual 16-core Neural Engine, 16GB of unified memory configurable up to 32GB, memory bandwidth up to 170GB/s; Apple says M6 brings up to 4x faster AI performance versus the previous-generation Mac mini with M4. M5 Pro: up-to-18-core CPU, up-to-20-core GPU, up to 64GB of unified memory with 307GB/s of bandwidth. M5 Max: 18-core CPU, up-to-40-core GPU, up to 128GB of unified memory. M5 Ultra: up-to-36-core CPU, up-to-80-core GPU, up to 512GB of unified memory with 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth; Apple says Mac Studio brings up to 4.3x faster AI performance (Apple testing). Thunderbolt 5 with RDMA lets multiple Mac Studio systems be clustered for up to 3x faster distributed AI inference versus a single system. Mac Studio with 512GB of unified memory is coming in late October. Starting prices: Mac mini with M6 $899, with M5 Pro $1,699; Mac Studio with M5 Max $2,499, with M5 Ultra $5,499. The release does not name the foundry or process node.
quarterly_data.figure: M6 and M5 Ultra launched (available September 22); M5 Ultra up to 512GB unified memory at 1.2TB/s; 512GB Mac Studio coming in late October; Mac mini from $899, Mac Studio from $2,499

quarterly_data.quarter: Apple press release: Apple introduces M6 and M5 Ultra for a big leap in (08-25-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Apple debuted M6 (in the new Mac mini) and M5 Ultra (in the new Mac Studio) on August 25, 2026. M6 is Apple's first 2-nanometer chip; Sri Santhanam, Apple's vice president of Silicon Engineering Group: 'Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth'. M6 has a 12-core CPU (2 super cores, 4 performance cores, 6 efficiency cores; up to 1.2x faster multithreaded than M5), a 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core (a nearly 30 percent increase in peak GPU compute for AI versus M5), a Dual 16-core Neural Engine (up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations), up to 32GB of unified memory and up to 170GB/s of bandwidth (a 10 percent increase over M5). M5 Ultra is Apple's first quad-die architecture: UltraFusion connects two dual-die M5 Max chips, increasing inter-die bandwidth to over 4.4TB/s and connection density by over 6x, so the four dies behave as a single unified processor. M5 Ultra has an up-to-36-core CPU (12 super cores and 24 performance cores), an up-to-80-core GPU with Neural Accelerators (up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI of M3 Ultra), a 32-core Neural Engine, and up to 512GB of unified memory at 1.2TB/s (50 percent higher than M3 Ultra). Apple calls M5 Ultra its most powerful chip ever (company claim). The release does not name the foundry.
quarterly_data.figure: M6: first 2 nm Apple chip, 12-core CPU / 12-core GPU, up to 170GB/s; M5 Ultra: quad-die via UltraFusion, inter-die bandwidth over 4.4TB/s, connection density over 6x, up to 512GB at 1.2TB/s

quarterly_data.quarter: Apple press release: Apple debuts iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are powered by A20 Pro, 'built using the latest 2-nanometer process technology': 50 percent more memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, a new 6-core CPU with integrated Neural Accelerators, a new 7-core GPU up to 40 percent faster than A19 Pro, and a Dual 16-core Neural Engine with 32 total cores for double the AI processing power of A19 Pro. Packaging change: A20 Pro 'introduces custom packaging inspired by M-series Apple silicon that places the silicon die side by side with the memory, removing the memory from the thermal path of the chip', so A20 Pro attaches directly to a next-generation vapor chamber (three times more surface area than on iPhone 17 Pro; up to a 40 percent gain in sustained performance). Both models carry N1, an Apple-designed wireless networking chip (Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread), and iPhone 18 Pro introduces C2, Apple's next-generation cellular modem system (meaningfully faster uploads than C1X while consuming 15 percent less energy; now supports mmWave in the U.S.). Pre-orders begin September 12 with availability September 18 in more than 65 countries and regions (20 more on September 25); iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 and iPhone 18 Pro Max at $1,299, in 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB capacities. The release does not name the foundry.
quarterly_data.figure: A20 Pro on 2-nanometer; 50 percent more memory bandwidth than A19 Pro; die side by side with memory in new package; C2 modem 15 percent less energy; available September 18; from $1,199

quarterly_data.quarter: Apple press release: Apple unveils iPhone Duo (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Apple introduced iPhone Duo, 'the first foldable iPhone', with a 7.6-inch inner display (50 percent larger than iPhone 18 Pro Max) and a 5.4-inch outer display. It is powered by A20 Pro (the same chip as the iPhone 18 Pro models, built on the latest 2-nanometer process technology) in 'a new chip package inspired by M-series Apple silicon' that connects A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber, for up to 35 percent better sustained performance than iPhone 17 Pro; dual-battery design, N1 wireless chip and C2 cellular modem, eSIM-only worldwide. CEO John Ternus: 'iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original.' Pre-orders begin October 16 with availability October 23 in more than 70 countries and regions (28 more on October 30); starts at $1,999 in 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB capacities; ships with iOS 27.1.
quarterly_data.figure: first foldable iPhone; A20 Pro (2-nanometer); availability October 23; starts at $1,999

quarterly_data.quarter: Apple press release: Siri AI, a profoundly more capable and personal assistant, (09-14-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Siri AI began rolling out in beta in English with Apple's 2027 software releases (French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish next month). The new capabilities are 'powered by the next generation of Apple Foundation Models, custom-built in collaboration with Google and its Gemini models', and 'these latest models run on device and on servers using Private Cloud Compute'; systemwide dictation uses Apple's most advanced on-device model, AFM Core Advanced. Server-side features (Siri AI, intelligent photo editing tools, Image Playground, AFM 3 Cloud models in Shortcuts) are subject to daily usage limits that 'may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand', and 'expanded access to such features will be available for a fee in the future'. Siri AI will not be available initially in the EU on iOS, iPadOS and watchOS, and Siri AI and the other new Apple Intelligence features will not be available in China while Apple works through regulatory requirements.
quarterly_data.figure: Siri AI beta rolling out; models built with Google Gemini, run on device and on Private Cloud Compute servers; server features usage-limited, paid expanded access planned

quarterly_data.signal: Memory supply-demand view (Memory EVP Jaejune Kim): with Agentic AI spreading, token consumption has grown exponentially, driving an unprecedented rise in demand for AI servers and general computing servers; AI frontier model developers short of hyperscaler cloud capacity are turning to neocloud providers, which have become major buyers from server OEMs, and frontier model developers are increasingly approaching Samsung directly to secure memory, sharing mid-to-long-term forecasts and requesting multi-year supply agreements. Mobile/PC demand is moderating as customers raise end-product prices, but additional demand for server DRAM, SSDs and HBM is far exceeding it, so the supply-demand gap next year 'will become much wider'; customers' demand is outgrowing supply despite production increases, and DRAM and NAND product mix will be optimised pre-emptively. With the lead time from new fab construction to wafer output exceeding three and a half years, management believes a significant increase in incremental supply is unlikely through 2028: unmet 2026 demand is likely to carry over, constraints are expected to be even more severe in 2027 than in 2026, and the shortage is expected to persist through 2028 (limited visibility beyond 2029). Capacity approach: clean-room capacity first through pre-emptive investment, then equipment installed flexibly with demand.

quarterly_data.signal: Memory multi-year supply contracts (Memory EVP Jaejune Kim): Samsung signs multi-year supply agreements on a five-year term, renegotiated annually with an option to add one more year (rolling basis). Agreements are already finalized with the top five global data center customers, and talks with five additional major accounts are in the final stages; almost all major customers want long-term supply, and existing contract holders are seeking additional volume. Samsung plans to allocate approximately 60% to 70% of total capacity to long-term contracts, keeping capacity for customers without multi-year contracts, and expects DRAM and NAND volumes under multi-year contracts to 'easily account for 60% to 70%' of planned capacity once pending contracts close. Priority goes to customers accepting mutually binding terms with committed demand. The contracts require substantial advance payments maintained over the contract period; Samsung has already received one-fourth of these payments and expects the balance to grow (further detail under NDA). Pricing is differentiated by customer segment and product, with minimum price floors set for conventional products to cover future investment risk; Samsung says it keeps a balanced customer portfolio without over-reliance on any single customer. CFO: customer prepayments on memory LTAs may affect free cash flow.

The 2026 capex budget is raised to USD 2 billion from USD 1.5 billion to support growing customer demand in silicon photonics and advanced packaging. CFO: the Board approved nearly USD 5 billion of capex over the next two to three years - USD 5 billion to be spent across 2026 and 2027, with 2028 to be determined by future phase decisions. Singapore P4 gets a cleanroom and equipment to expand silicon photonics capacity; in Tainan, construction of 12A P7 and P8 (foundation shells) will let UMC scale advanced packaging, with P7 prepared for advanced packaging. CEO: construction lead times are roughly greater than 20 months, putting meaningful capacity in the 2028-2029 timeframe; detailed schedules will follow once equipment installers and contractors confirm.

quarterly_data.signal: AI-related revenue (CEO Jason Wang): UMC's AI-related business is driven by specialty solutions - power management, connectivity, FPGA - plus the growing advanced packaging and silicon photonics business, and has begun to become an important contributor to growth in 2026. AI-related revenue is projected to be close to approximately USD 300 million this year, and UMC expects it to exceed USD 1 billion in three years. Silicon photonics and advanced packaging, still at an early stage, have the highest CAGR; connectivity and power management are major contributors. In the near term UMC sees upside in silicon photonics, power and FPGA-related products, particularly in 40nm and 65nm technologies.
quarterly_data.figure: AI-related revenue close to approximately USD 300 million in 2026; expected to exceed USD 1 billion in three years

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon photonics (CEO Jason Wang): earlier this month UMC announced its first mass production delivery of a 12-inch photonics IC to a customer, which it calls a major milestone demonstrating high-volume silicon photonics manufacturing on 12-inch wafers; the silicon photonics platform is to be available for general customer use in 2027. UMC says it is the first to offer a 12-inch solution, with better process control and performance than 8-inch competitors (lower propagation loss and better yield, demonstrated to customers). In TFLN, UMC says it has the world's first TFLN modulator in production and is developing 40G per lane and beyond, supporting beyond-400G use cases. TFLN components can be combined with UMC's silicon photonics PICs through advanced packaging: UMC can offer optical I/O interposers with PICs and provide TFLN components for CPO solutions.
quarterly_data.figure: first mass-production delivery of a 12-inch photonics IC; platform general availability 2027; TFLN 40G per lane in development, beyond 400G

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging (CEO Jason Wang): UMC started with interposer solutions and RF SOI 3D IC and chiplet solutions and now offers more, and projects its addressable market to more than double by 2030 as it expands from 2.5D interposers with DTC and discrete DTC to wafer-to-wafer stacking and memory-to-memory stacking. More than ten active customers and over 35 new products are in discussion, with expected tape-outs in 2026 and early 2027; a high percentage of those products are DTC, which is a significant portion. UMC has entered production for 3D wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding, bridge die and discrete DTC. It is not positioning as a direct CoWoS alternative, and works across the entire ecosystem rather than with a single partner. CEO: 'We believe we are ahead of our peers in advanced packaging, which is leading to share gains and many new opportunities.'
quarterly_data.figure: addressable market to more than double by 2030; more than ten active customers; over 35 new products in discussion; tape-outs 2026 and early 2027

The business model will be accretive to current financials as it ramps, with most meaningful revenue as volume ramps in 2028 and beyond. Supply reduction plus inventory normalization are giving more visibility. The CEO sees this cycle as different from the previous broad-based one, with AI the primary growth driver.

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 drivers (Co-CEO Zhao Haijun): the shipment increase was mainly driven by surging demand for peripheral chips brought by AI plus customer pull-ins - SMIC accelerated wafers close to shipment and slowed new wafer starts, and capacity built in prior years (about 16 months on average from tool move-in to customer release) came up to volume. SMIC allocated more capacity to tight segments, so AI peripheral chips, computer and tablet, and industrial and automotive revenue each grew about 40% QoQ; customer pull-ins lifted smartphone, consumer electronics and connectivity / IoT revenue 8%, 16% and 13%. Gross margin rose 5.2 points on higher blended ASP and better-than-expected utilisation, offsetting higher depreciation. SMIC plans to report AI peripheral chips as a separate application category next quarter or later.
quarterly_data.figure: AI peripheral, computer and tablet, industrial and automotive revenue about +40% QoQ

quarterly_data.signal: Q3 2026 outlook beyond the revenue / margin guidance (Co-CEO Zhao Haijun): shipments expected to keep growing and prices to remain resilient; utilisation including newly added capacity expected to stay around 95%; the gross-margin rise is after offsetting incremental Q3 depreciation and peak summer power costs. Q2 shipments were largely wafers started in Q1 or Q4 2025 at old prices; SMIC prices from wafer start, so the new prices show more in Q3. Q3 will not repeat Q2's pull-ins, to keep the line running smoothly. Orders are already received into Q4 and year-end; he sees no possibility of price cuts this year ('at least maintained').
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 utilisation around 95% including new capacity

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and supply (Co-CEO Zhao Haijun): SMIC added 8000 12-inch-equivalent wafers of monthly capacity in Q2 and adds capacity at a steady, even pace of a similar amount per quarter; it keeps 5% of capacity for R&D, so utilisation of about 95% is essentially the ceiling. Supply falls short of demand, also over the long term, in AI- and compute-related peripheral chips for data-center and compute boards - logic, BCD and optical-module transmit / receive chips. Overseas, some companies have stopped making specialty low-density memory and flash, and SMIC's capacity there is 'far from meeting demand', with prices rising. Customers of smartphone chips and display drivers (DDIC) for TVs and monitors can no longer get capacity and are negotiating future capacity and prices; customers' requests to reserve capacity have grown greatly since February, and SMIC is adjusting existing fab space to add more equipment.

quarterly_data.signal: Pricing (Co-CEO Zhao Haijun): SMIC does not announce across-the-board increases but negotiates with customers; around February-March 2026 it agreed partial price increases in its tightest, supply-constrained segments, with no increases so far for smartphone chips or display drivers, where customers are struggling. He said that after the more than 4-point drag from higher depreciation, Q2 gross margin was about 9% to 10% higher than Q1 as the Q1-negotiated prices took effect; price increases contributed more to margin than product-mix optimisation (e.g., shifting logic capacity to MCU or specialty memory, and LCD-driver capacity to NAND flash), and new capacity is pre-ordered by customers and fully loaded at good prices. Further increases will follow supply tightness and are expected mainly in lower-priced consumer, smartphone and display-driver products, though not by a large amount this year. 'SMIC is never the first to raise prices, nor raises them the most.' Capacity allocation favours long-term strategic customers with prior commitments first.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 gross margin about 9% to 10% above Q1 before the depreciation drag (Co-CEO)

quarterly_data.signal: Depreciation (CFO Wu Junfeng / Co-CEO Zhao Haijun): 2026 depreciation is expected to rise about 30% year-on-year to close to US$5 billion (Zhao: about US$4.9-5.0 billion for the year), increasing by roughly US$120-140 million each quarter and weighing about 4% to 5% on gross margin per quarter; H1 depreciation was about US$2.3 billion. Under previously announced expansion plans depreciation would peak in 2027, but expansion plans are being adjusted to customer orders, and depreciation is expected to rise further after 2027, so the peak timing is uncertain. Zhao: SMIC will keep protecting its gross margin while expanding.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 depreciation up about 30% YoY

quarterly_data.signal: AI demand for mature nodes (Co-CEO Zhao Haijun): AI first drives the two ends - standard logic for compute and very mature analog, where 8-inch demand growth 'far exceeds imagination' - while 40nm / 28nm is pulled along only by spillover. Power supply and power management demand is very large: in a rack with 72 GPUs plus other components, power supply / power management parts alone can exceed 16,000. BCD demand and prices remain firm and supply-short, with demand visible to the end of next year; 48V high-voltage, high-current parts (needing 80-100V withstand) are mainly on 8-inch, while some single high-volume parts are moving to 12-inch. Smartphone inventory 'should be gradually getting high' after pull-ins, and customers in consumer and panel drivers are starting to stock up for next year, fearing capacity shortages and higher supply-chain, packaging-test and materials costs.

quarterly_data.signal: CY2026 outlook: Applied expects to grow its semiconductor equipment business more than 20% this calendar year, with demand weighted to the second half and availability of customer cleanroom space the key factor pacing investment; largest customers are giving longer-term visibility and strong growth momentum is expected to carry into 2027 (CEO: '27 is shaping up to be another strong year). CEO believes global semiconductor industry revenues can potentially reach $1 trillion in 2026, several years earlier than prior predictions. Leading-edge foundry/logic, DRAM including HBM, and advanced packaging are expected to be the fastest-growing WFE segments in '26, '27 and the next several years, where Applied says it holds strong #1 process equipment positions. NAND is forecast for modest growth and to remain less than 10% of WFE; ICAPS WFE is now seen approximately flat year-on-year both globally and in China (last quarter Applied expected China and ICAPS WFE to be down a little on capacity digestion), with the ICAPS market growing mid- to high single digits longer term. Asked by an analyst whether the earlier ~15% WFE-intensity framing still holds, the CEO said WFE intensity has grown to around 15%, but that Applied's longer-term composition model now differs from the earlier 1/3 leading-edge foundry/logic, 1/3 ICAPS, 1/3 memory split because end-market growth rates have diverged - "it's time for a new growth framework" - with leading-edge foundry/logic and DRAM becoming significantly larger than ICAPS and other memory.
quarterly_data.figure: semiconductor equipment business to grow more than 20% in CY2026; industry revenues potentially $1 trillion in 2026; NAND less than 10% of WFE

quarterly_data.signal: Supply and capacity: CFO said leading-edge foundry/logic and DRAM capacity is essentially full and prices have increased, semiconductor factory utilization is rising across all device types, and Applied is tracking higher planned capex from cloud service providers. This year's shipments are metered by cleanroom in leading edge and DRAM - customers found more space to add DRAM and leading-logic capacity than planned a quarter ago but have exhausted most of it; a number of DRAM and leading-logic factories are scheduled to come online in '27, the count of new factory projects Applied tracks keeps rising each quarter, and Applied expects to "go into next year still in a constrained position." Applied has nearly doubled its system manufacturing capacity over the past several years and still has prepositioned space to scale much higher; it increased inventory by nearly $500 million year-over-year for rising build plans (inventory days approximately 153, not expected to rise much) and is giving its approximately 2,000 suppliers longer visibility and specific bills of material. CEO said customers now give significantly longer-term visibility with specific configurations because supply chain and service-engineer training take time.
quarterly_data.figure: inventory up nearly $500 million year-over-year; approximately 2,000 suppliers; inventory days approximately 153

quarterly_data.signal: Leading-edge logic: customers are adding capacity at FinFET nodes while ramping gate-all-around nodes, which grow Applied's available market considerably and give multiple points of share gain. CEO said Applied is #1 and on track to capture more than 50% of its served market in gate-all-around and wiring, including backside power, and is #1 in deposition, conductor etch and packaging. Applied plans to launch more than a dozen new products in 2026, including 3 for advanced logic and DRAM announced the week of the call: the Viva radical treatment system (angstrom-level engineering of nanosheet surfaces for faster gate-all-around transistors), Sym3 Z Magnum (newest Sym3 etch variant for critical etch steps in gate-all-around transistors and advanced DRAM) and the Spectral ALD system (selective deposition of monocrystalline moly, reducing contact resistance in advanced logic devices by up to 15%). Applied is leading the transition from ALD tungsten to ALD moly in logic contact formation, while copper PVD steps keep growing and remain an order of magnitude larger than ALD moly.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 50% of served market in gate-all-around and wiring; more than a dozen new products in 2026; contact resistance reduced by up to 15%

quarterly_data.signal: Process diagnostics and control: Applied expects revenue from its cold field emission (CFE) eBeam technology to double this calendar year to more than $1 billion, making it one of the fastest-growing businesses in 2026; CEO cites the highest resolution and 10x faster imaging, says new material-characterization products will be announced, and has very high confidence the growth continues at a high rate in '27. quarterly_data.figure: CFE eBeam revenues to double this calendar year to more than $1 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Data center share of wafer starts (CFO): Applied previously said more than 20% of leading-edge wafer starts were directed to data center; this year data center passes PCs in consumption of leading-edge wafer starts, and Applied moved up its forecast so that data center surpasses smartphones in 2029. CFO's rough model: traditional data center (racks, file servers) growing between 10% and 20% and AI-related components growing between 30% and 40%, giving something north of 20% overall. CEO, citing discussions with his largest customers' CEOs and R&D leaders (who talk about extremely high compound annual growth rates), said he thinks AI data center demand is a significant wave that will last over a longer period, and expects '27 to also be a very strong year.
quarterly_data.figure: previously more than 20% of leading-edge wafer starts directed to data center; data center to surpass smartphones in 2029; AI-related components growing between 30% and 40%

quarterly_data.signal: Applied Global Services: record Q1 revenue grew 15% year-over-year on the recast basis (200-millimeter systems moved to Semiconductor Systems), with non-GAAP gross margin up 210 basis points and operating margin up 320 basis points; the Q2 guide implies approximately over 12%, almost 13% year-over-year AGS growth. CEO sees an opportunity for AGS to grow faster as customers ramp gate-all-around, backside power and complex memory architectures.

Akara, Lam's latest-generation conductor etch system (printed 'Aqara'/'Acara' in this transcript), doubled its installed base over the past year and won production tool-of-record positions for EUV and high-aspect-ratio etch in advanced DRAM and foundry logic. Critical dimensions in foundry logic shrink roughly 10 to 20% node to node, and in next-generation gate-all-around devices the number of applications using Akara should grow by roughly two times, including critical front-end silicon etch. Drivers still ahead: 'Backside power is still to come, and it's gonna be a driver for us', along with the later move to CFET and more advanced packaging across leading-edge foundry at future nodes. Lam has refreshed its conductor and dielectric etch lines and launched Moly.
quarterly_data.figure: GAA = roughly $1 billion incremental SAM per 100,000 wafer starts per month; Akara installed base doubled; Akara applications roughly two times in next-gen GAA; CDs shrink roughly 10 to 20% per node

The growth figure covers both HBM and more complex packaging in advanced foundry logic ('we've lumped it together'), and Lam's copper plating, etch and dielectric gap-fill tools are used to package all device types. AI applications are the driver in memory - there is a lack of capacity in DRAM and NAND driving much of the demand profile Ichor sees - and foundry and logic are also strong this year. Fiscal 2025 growth came primarily from etch and deposition, partially offset by softening EUV build rates and decreased demand in certain trailing-edge markets. EUV is roughly flat quarter over quarter and expected to pick up late in 2026: the lithography customer still has inventory to digest, which Ichor expects to be digested by roughly Q3 with some uptick in Q4 (with some unknowns), and that customer expects growth in the second half of 2026 into 2027. Ichor's revenue forecast is starting to match what its two biggest customers are saying, which management reads as a good indication that inventory levels are coming down, need to be replenished and have really burnt through from the last cycle; gas panels, the bulk of Ichor's business, carry little inventory, unlike the non-configurable EUV system.

Asked by an analyst whether the 15% second-half gross margin target (the crosswalk he cited from Ichor's slides published last month) still holds, with incremental progress in Q2 and a pickup in the second half, the CEO said that is how he would model it; he declined to put a timeline on the 18% to 20% gross margin level an analyst cited as previous targets but expects significant earnings leverage moving through 2027 as components kick in.

Relocating a portion of machining assets to these sites temporarily reduces capacity for those components but will not gate Ichor's ability to support customer demand. The Malaysia facility is two miles from Ichor's current second-largest facility, which builds essentially every weldment; it adds machining and components capacity for a ramp expected to continue through 2026 into 2027, with headwinds baked into Q1 and tailwinds seen in 2027. The CEO sees little to no risk in Mexico, which already runs pretty high volumes, and a little higher qualification risk in Malaysia. quarterly_data.signal: FIRST HARD SIZING OF THE CPO TEST MARKET, PLUS WHO WINS WHICH INSERTION (CEO Greg Smith): the test-equipment TAM for silicon photonics co-packaged optics is about $100 million in 2026 and is expected to be between $300 million and $700 million by 2028, reaching about a billion dollars of test equipment by 2030 (optical alignment, interface hardware and material handling are a separate TAM). Today it is 'a very concentrated market' - one customer and a very small number of devices drive most of the 2026 capital intensity. A CPO device has four major optical test insertions: (1) the photonics wafer, (2) the silicon photonics wafer with the electronic ICs bonded to it, (3) the singulated optical engine dielets with the mounting plate for FAU alignment, (4) the assembled CPO device. On this first device at this first customer, 'Advantest is strongest in insertion one, Teradyne is strongest in insertion two, a Taiwanese supplier is strongest in insertion three, and Teradyne is strongest in insertion four.' Management flags scaling pain as the reason for 'increasing excitement about copper networking for scale-up' and for NPO, which avoids the yield risk of a full CPO device.

quarterly_data.signal: Teradyne announced Iris 100, which it calls a production-ready ("production-proven") optical test platform for microLED devices. It measures every individual emitter in an array with a spectrometer and high-resolution camera (spectral response, per-pixel luminance and uniformity), integrates directly with the Teradyne UltraFLEXplus platform for combined optical and electrical test, runs on Teradyne's IG-XL software to detect dead/stuck pixels and cluster defects early in manufacturing, and uses a NIST-traceable calibration workflow to correlate lots, wafers and manufacturing sites. It supports wafer and final test, with a roadmap to support photodetector test in the same insertion. Target devices are microLED arrays for AR microdisplays and optical data interconnects for AI data center architectures, which the company says contain hundreds of thousands to millions of individual emitters. Shannon Poulin, president of the Semiconductor Test division, said "MicroLED is shifting from lab to volume production for both AR microdisplays and, increasingly, optical interconnects, which are becoming foundational to how AI data centers scale beyond copper," and that Iris 100 delivers per-emitter test at production throughput "today on test infrastructure our customers already run at scale." Teradyne says it follows the Photon 100 introduction for silicon photonics and co-packaged optics test earlier this year. No customers named.

quarterly_data.signal: Teradyne announced the launch of three new instruments for its UltraFLEXplus platform, designed for AI and data center semiconductor testing. UltraPort-PCIe6: which Teradyne calls the industry's first high-speed I/O protocol ATE solution for PCIe Gen6 interfaces, 64 Gbps (PAM-4) across 32 lanes per instrument, with a server-class compute backend scaling to 2TB of memory; it supports mission-mode testing and high-speed I/O scan so test coverage can shift to earlier insertions, improving Known Good Die confidence and reducing waste of high-value HBM and advanced packaging assemblies. No customers named.

quarterly_data.signal: 2026 logic and industry outlook: management expects Entegris to benefit from node transitions in both logic and memory. Rising demand for two-nanometer devices should meaningfully lift wafer output through 2026, and that node carries both higher content per wafer and strong share for Entegris. Advanced logic fab utilization is already near 100%, and customers are investing aggressively in more capacity. At the most advanced logic node, Entegris has secured strong POR (position of record) positions in CMP consumables, advanced deposition and implant materials, liquid purification and filtration, and wafer handling. The team is now focused on winning incremental share and PORs at subsequent advanced nodes. Separately, the CEO said it takes time to grow two-nanometer and to transition to new nodes such as 1.4 nanometer. Management expects 'middish single-digit' industry MSI (wafer starts) growth in 2026 and strong WFE growth. Fab construction CapEx should grow modestly after last year's high single-digit decline, weighted to the second half, with a bigger acceleration in 2027 as work starts on new fabs. Management flagged ongoing memory shortages as a possible second-half 2026 risk for mainstream end markets; guidance assumes no impact.
quarterly_data.figure: middish single-digit industry MSI growth expected in 2026; advanced logic utilization near 100%

quarterly_data.signal: NAND: the move from roughly 250 layers to approximately 300 layers is under way. Management expects more than 20% NAND bit growth in 2026, driven mainly by higher-layer, higher-capacity NAND rather than a big increase in wafer starts. Entegris expects a double-digit increase in its NAND content per wafer as customers move to higher layer counts and adopt new materials such as moly and selective etch. It has won strong POR positions in NAND deposition materials, CMP and selective etch. NAND utilization is around 85%, and layer-count increases are absorbing most of the remaining 15% of capacity, with fewer new wafer starts. If demand stays strong, flash makers will likely need to add significant fab capacity, setting up higher NAND MSI growth in 2027. The CEO said Entegris gains from both layer growth and wafer growth, with slightly more from a full wafer start.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 20% NAND bit growth expected in 2026; double-digit increase in NAND content per wafer; NAND utilization around 85%

quarterly_data.signal: DRAM, HBM and advanced packaging: DRAM capacity was nearly fully utilized at the end of 2025, and management expects it to stay that way through 2026. More DRAM is shifting from standalone DDR5 into HBM, which adds some content per wafer, though less than a new wafer start would. Management expects tight supply in HBM, DDR5 and advanced packaging to require additional fab capacity heading into 2027. Entegris is gaining traction in DRAM and HBM, particularly with CMP consumables and advanced packaging solutions. The CEO said advanced packaging revenue grew nicely in 2025, to 'roughly a $100 million plus minus', and should keep growing in 2026. Several product lines for advanced packaging are sampling now and more will sample later in the year, so the larger benefit is expected in 2027 and beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: advanced packaging revenue roughly $100 million (2025), expected to keep growing in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and capex: the multiyear manufacturing capex cycle that began in 2022 is complete. Capex was $299 million in 2025 (approximately 9% of sales) and is expected to fall to $250 million in 2026, returning longer term to approximately 7% to 8% of sales. Management said the new capacity plus the existing base can deliver significantly more than $1 billion in incremental revenue with limited further investment. The Taiwan facility is still ramping, and the Colorado facility should substantially complete key customer product qualifications in 2026. Entegris exited its Chester, Pennsylvania facility in Q4 and expects to rationalize at least one additional facility in 2026. Free cash flow was $404 million in 2025, a 12.7% margin (up nearly 300 basis points year over year). Net leverage ended 2025 at 3.8 times, against a target of below 3.5 times by the end of 2026, and Entegris paid down $300 million of its term loan during 2025.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 capex $299 million; 2026 capex expected $250 million; capacity supports significantly more than $1 billion incremental revenue; 2025 free cash flow $404 million (12.7% margin)

quarterly_data.quarter: JX Advanced Metals annual securities report: FY2026 (06-24-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Management's view (annual securities report): the semiconductor logic and memory market keeps growing on the rapid spread of generative AI; because leading-edge logic has more wiring layers and uses more sputtering targets, management expects its sputtering-target sales volume to grow faster than the logic and memory market, while ever finer wiring is raising needs for CVD/ALD thin-film deposition. AI servers use many of its Semiconductor Materials products - sputtering targets for on-chip wiring, InP substrates for optical communications, high-purity tantalum powder for tantalum capacitors and magnetic-material targets for high-capacity HDDs - and management also expects target demand to grow in packaging (inter-chip wiring such as TSV and RDL, and chiplet interconnects). In ICT Materials, adoption of titanium copper in AI-server connectors is expanding rapidly and demand for leak sensors that detect coolant leaks inside AI servers is expected to grow. Priorities: expand capacity and productivity for data-center and AI-server products (semiconductor sputtering targets, magnetic-material sputtering targets, InP substrates, tantalum powder, titanium copper), and create next-generation global top-share products in advanced materials and advanced packaging (the JOINT3 next-generation packaging consortium, CVD/ALD materials, CdZnTe substrates for medical and sensor uses).

quarterly_data.quarter: Dai Nippon Printing IR Day: DNP Group IR-Day FY2026 (07-13-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Photomask business plan (Nakanishi, head of Fine Device Operations): DNP aims for average annual photomask sales growth of more than 15% through FY2030 (the fiscal year ending March 2031), driven by commercialising cutting-edge technologies. After JPY20 billion of capex in April 2023 - March 2026 it is raising its photomask capex plan for April 2026 - March 2029 to JPY70 billion, covering EUV masks, nanoimprint and production capability from advanced areas to the volume zone, and expects sales in cutting-edge areas alone to rise by JPY24 billion in the year ending March 2029 versus the year ended March 2025. Management (Q&A): it cannot break down the JPY70 billion, but as EUV equipment is extremely expensive 'it is reasonable to assume' EUV accounts for a substantial proportion; capex for nanoimprint mass production is not yet included and will be decided once customers indicate production timing and volumes; the large photomask sales increase projected in its materials for the years ending March 2028 and March 2029 reflects capacity expansion through large-scale capex; growth is now forecast above last year's plan because EUV-related business has become more tangible and merchant sales volume is expected to be greater than anticipated last year, from higher order volumes at existing customers.
quarterly_data.figure: Photomask sales growth more than 15% a year through FY2030 (year ending March 2031); photomask capex JPY 70 billion (April 2026 - March 2029); cutting-edge sales +JPY 24 billion

quarterly_data.quarter: Dai Nippon Printing IR Day: DNP Group IR-Day FY2026 (07-13-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: EUV and nanoimprint status (Nakanishi): DNP 'successfully completed Rapidus' NEDO (New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization) project as planned' and, building on that experience, has established the technical capabilities and manufacturing foundation for 2 nm-generation EUV masks; it aims to be a partner with reliable supply capacity in advanced masks, including EUV masks, as device makers outsource advanced logic and memory photomasks. In nanoimprint it has developed a 10 nm line-width template equivalent to the 1.4 nm generation, now under evaluation by several customers, and will keep expanding its presence 'as the sole mask supplier'. Management says these technologies come from more than 10 years of R&D and upfront investment and from collaboration with partners including KIOXIA, Rapidus, imec and Canon, plus long-standing photomask joint ventures.
quarterly_data.figure: 2 nm-generation EUV mask capability established; 10 nm line-width nanoimprint template (1.4 nm generation) in evaluation by several customers

quarterly_data.quarter: Dai Nippon Printing IR Day: DNP Group IR-Day FY2026 (07-13-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Photomask demand view (Nakanishi; management Q&A): DNP expects the semiconductor market to grow from about USD770 billion in 2025 to about USD2 trillion in 2035 (about 10% a year), driven by AI semiconductors for data centers, advanced logic and advanced memory; in the merchant photomask market, advanced-node demand expands significantly as miniaturisation needs more masks, while the over-14 nm volume segment grows steadily. Customers putting their limited resources into cutting-edge products outsource previous-generation masks, and DNP expects outsourcing of products one or two generations behind the leading edge to increase rapidly; even EUV processes include non-EUV layers that customers will outsource, and high-end optical masks at the EUV boundary will be progressively outsourced. EUV demand 'has yet to take off', but demand is rising steadily in the high-resolution segment for the generation immediately preceding EUV, where DNP is securing orders; legacy-node masks were affected by reduced smartphone production due to memory shortages, but DNP is securing orders for industrial and automotive applications. AI investment, now extending to physical AI, is expected to lift orders for both EUV masks and related non-EUV layers; DNP will meet staffing needs by reallocating people across the group as well as hiring.
quarterly_data.figure: Semiconductor market from about USD 770 billion (2025) to about USD 2 trillion (2035), about 10% a year

quarterly_data.quarter: Dai Nippon Printing IR Day: DNP Group IR-Day FY2026 (07-13-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Group plan detail (Senior Managing Director Miyake; management Q&A): operating profit is to grow about 9% a year from JPY101 billion (year ended March 2026) to JPY130 billion (year ending March 2029). Half of sales in the year to March 2026 came from the six focus businesses, which are to reach 57% by the year to March 2029, while businesses for reforming, cut from 48% of sales (year to March 2023) to 17% (year to March 2026), are to fall to 9%; the six focus businesses' total sales are to grow about 10% a year, from JPY510 billion (year to March 2023) and JPY606 billion (year to March 2026) to JPY808 billion (year to March 2029), with information security going from JPY187 billion to JPY271 billion (13% CAGR). More than 60% of the JPY200 billion growth capex goes to Electronics, especially semiconductors; because EUV, nanoimprint and glass cores are set to enter the mass-production phase during April 2026 - March 2029, DNP plans continued capex and possibly further capacity investment. Q&A: capex is not fixed at JPY200 billion and, through flexible allocation, semiconductor growth investment could exceed JPY120 billion. Structural reforms are to add JPY5 billion or more in the year ending March 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: Focus businesses 57% of sales by the year ending March 2029; more than 60% of JPY 200 billion growth capex to Electronics; semiconductor growth investment could exceed JPY 120 billion

quarterly_data.quarter: Dai Nippon Printing IR Day: DNP Group IR-Day FY2026 (07-13-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Digital Interface (Miyake): its main products are metal masks, increasingly for OLED, and optical films. Because of the semiconductor memory shortage some manufacturers find it difficult to produce smartphones in the short term, so DNP's metal-mask order volume is declining; smartphone OLED panel shipments are projected to decline in FY2026 (as DNP labels it; DNP's FY2026 runs April 2026 - March 2027) because of the memory shortage and to grow thereafter, for an average annual growth rate of 3%. Foldables could raise the OLED area per phone about three times, lifting metal-mask shipments; notebook PCs and tablets are forecast to grow about 29% a year and TV screens of 65 inches and larger about 6% a year in area. DNP will use its G8-size production line across more OLED panel types and raise utilisation of the line installed last September mainly for surface materials for 65-inch and larger panels; the goal is about 5% average annual sales growth.

Only about $165 million of cash sits outside the joint ventures, so 'if we need cash, we would either issue debt or a line of credit... Not likely to use equity'.
